article.title: FDR, Trump, and Fascism
article.author: Walter G. Moss
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. According to the English newspaper The Guardian , in the late summer of 2026, “Donald Trump . . . declared himself to be the ‘greatest’ US president ever.” Some others have proclaimed him the greatest of our lifetime. My own assessment— shared by many presidential experts? The worst president of my octogenarian life. Take just one comparison, that with FDR, President Franklin D. Roosevelt. According to a review of historian William I. Hitchcock’s new book, A Shadow Over the World: Franklin D. Roosevelt, the Rise of Fascism, and the Making of America’s World War II , “ the indelible feature of Roosevelt’s Presidency was his desire to protect democratic norms and processes amid crises, even as critics accused him of being a power-mad dictator or a Communist sympathizer.” In 1936, he proclaimed that “here in America we are waging a great and successful war. . . . It is a war for the survival of democracy. We are fighting to save a great and precious form of government for ourselves and for the world.” Hitchcock declares that this was “the thesis of the rest of his presidency.” Rather than protecting our “democratic norms,” Trump seems determined to tear them down. To take just one example, consider Trump’s recent ban of White House access for ‌journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico. And lest one thinks that FDR had no challenges to such norms, Hitchcock reminds us of “Americans’ embrace of eugenics and racism, anti-egalitarianism and antisemitism, nativism and illiberal politics,” and “the literal Fascism that took root in the U.S. during the thirties, when avowedly pro-Nazi organizations held mass rallies at Madison Square Garden and Henry Ford cozied up to Hitler.” Hitchcock adds that “during the thirties, anti-Communism was at least as powerful as antifascism in the U.S.” Related: Why Affirmative Action Needs to Continue One presidential scholar, Robert Dallek, commented that he wrote his biography of FDR “to remind people, especially a younger generation with limited knowledge of American history, of what great presidential leadership looks like.” Although both Hitchcock and Dallek admit that FDR had his flaws and faults—e.g, policies toward Jews, immigrants, and Nazi Germany—they think, as Dallek writes, that “neither Congress nor public opinion was as liberal or progressive as the president, and FDR often chose not to be too confrontational, which would have lessened his popular appeal.” And regarding “Roosevelt’s options in dealing with Stalin” in WW2, Dallek adds that they “were severely limited by political and geographical realities.” Dallek also had some thoughts about President Trump. In an earlier HNN interview he noted that he was “thinking of writing a book about democracy’s demagogues,” including “Huey Long and Father Coughlin [both often mentioned in his FDR biography], Joe McCarthy, George Wallace, and probably a closing chapter on Donald Trump, because I think he fits the pattern of these past demagogues.” In a December 2017 Newsweek essay Dallek stated that “it is clear Trump is unfit to serve,” and lawmakers should “invoke the 25th Amendment” to remove him from office.” In contrast to FDR, as Dallek observed, Trump sounds more like the “past demagogues” the scholar has mentioned—Long, Coughlin, Joe McCarthy, etc. In 1935, after Roosevelt proposed a “wealth tax,” William Randolph Hearst, whose papers and magazines circulated among millions of Americans, denounced it (sounding like the later McCarthy) as a “soak-the-successful” measure that was “essentially Communism.” And in 1944, running against Roosevelt for president, the Republican candidate Thomas Dewey charged that FDR’s New Deal was “Communist inspired.” Dallek also noted that among FDR’s “New Deal’s fiercest critics were many wealthy businessmen.” For example, the head of General Motors said, “with unemployment insurance no one would work; with old-age and survivors insurance no one would save; the result would be moral decay, financial bankruptcy and the collapse of the republic.” Billionaires are also among Trump’s supporters, and this should not surprise us since he is one and they (and he and his family) benefit the most from his policies . But capitalism before FDR was not especially favorable toward the working class, and Dallek observes that, like the progressives before him, he took “giant steps in humanizing the American industrial system.” Related: Obama, Trump and the Battle Over American Values Another difference between FDR and Trump is the people they surround themselves with, including those they bring into the government. One Trump critic has noted that in his second term, what is demanded is “complete loyalty to Trump.” FDR, however, surrounded himself with differing voices, including progressive ones (e.g., Interior Secretary Harold Ickes, Labor Secretary Frances Perkins, and his wife, Eleanor Roosevelt), as well as those more cautious. In summary, one can do no better than quote The Atlantic’s Jonathan Rauch , who after resisting the label “fascist” for Trump during his first term, concluded after a year into his second one: “Over Trump’s past year, what originally looked like an effort to make the government his personal plaything has drifted distinctly toward doctrinal and operational fascism.”
